Environment Impact Assessment for Delhi Metro Phase IV-2 Project 
 
 
1 A DELHI METRO RAIL COOPERATION LTD. 
 
EXECUTIVE SUMMARY  
A. INTRODUCTION 
The scope of Environmental Impact Assessment (EIA) included establishing environmental 
baseline, assess impacts resulting from pre-construction, construction and operation phases and 
propose safeguard measures for protection of environment. An environmental management plan 
was developed to mitigate the adverse impacts during construction and operation phases of the 
project. Cost of implementing the EMP and post -implementation environmental monitoring has 
been estimated. Rehabilitation and Resettlement is presented as part of a separate Social Impact 
Assessment (SIA) Report. 
The Ministry  of Environment Forests and Climate  Change (MoEF&CC), Government  of India, 
Notification of 14 th September 2006 and its  amendment dated 1 st December 2009 list projects 
that require environmental clearance. As per this Notification a metro rail project does not 
require environmental clearance from MoEF&CC. 
The scope of the study is framed as per Japan International Cooperation Agency (JICA) Guidelines 
for Environmental and Social Considerations (January 2022) (the JICA Guidelines). The objectives 
of the JICA guidelines are to encourage Project proponents to have appropriate consideration for 
environmental and social impacts, as well as to ensure that JICA’s support for examination of 
environmental and social considerations are conducted accordingly. 
B. PROJECT DESCRIPTION 
The EIA study covers the proposed metro corridors. Three metro corridors have been proposed 
in New Delhi to cater the requirement of the city viz. 
Corridor 1 is Inderlok to Indraprastha, Line 5 extension (Green line) which is 12.377km in length, 
Corridor 2 is Lajpat Nagar to Saket G Block, Line 11 (Gold line) which is 8.385 km in length and 
Corridor 3: Rithala–Narela-Nathupur, Line 1 Extension (Red line) which is 26.463 km in length. 
Total length of elevated portion is 34.896km out of which in 1.028 km in Corridor 1,8.385 km in 
Corridor 2  and 25.483 km in Corridor 3 . The length of underground section is 11.349 km in 
Corridor 1.0 km in Corridor 2 and 3, in this At Grade is 0.980 km in Corridor 3 only. 
Total 37 stations are proposed on the route out of which 8 stations are proposed on underground 
section, 28 stations are proposed on elevated section and 1 station is proposed as at grade.  
C. LEGAL, POLICY AND INSTITUTIONAL FRAMEWORK 
The project's execution will be overseen in accordance with the environmental laws, regulations, 
and standards at both the national and state levels. The proposed project will be implemented in 
compliance with the JICA Guidelines. These regulations necessitate the avoidance, minimization, 
and mitigation of potential environmental and social impacts.  
D. ALTERNATIVE ANALYSIS 
The proposed Delhi Metro Phase IV-2 project has been finalized after considering environmental 
and social concerns, considerations of traffic, integration with the  existing system and  
importantly, the overall economic and financial viability. The underlying principles for evaluation 
for each corridor  is without affecting the overall usefulness of the corridor. In the analysis of 
alternatives, a comparison of scenario with and without the project has also been made. 
Advantages and disadvantages have been spelt out. 
E. ENVIRONMENTAL BASELINE DATA

Environment Impact Assessment for Delhi Metro Phase IV-2 Project 
 
 
2 A DELHI METRO RAIL COOPERATION LTD. 
 
The environmental baseline data collected for EIA study includes physiography, geology and soils, 
ground water hydrology, flora and fauna, meteorology, air pollution, noise  and vibration as well 
as social economic environment.  
F. SCOPING 
The monitoring of environmental parameters has been conducted within the direct impact zone 
(Proposed ROW of 20m) and indirect zone (50 m) as is the usual practice for such projects.  The 
study has been essentially carried out in two parts: from primary and from secondary sources. 
Hence, we have collected primary data for dry season (May to June 2024 ) and wet season 
(September 2024 for ground water and surface water, flora and fauna only) as well as Secondary 
data (CPCB) for dry season i.e. March 2024 and Wet season data for July 2023.  
Field study has been conducted for collection of Environment Baseline Data (Primary Data) along 
the project alignment on key parameters like- Baseline Data for Physical Environment (Air, Water, 
Noise, Vibration Soil, fauna and flora, Land etc.) 
G.  SURVEY AND ANALYSIS RESULTS 
 
Physiography: The physiography of Delhi is dominated by the River Yamuna, the Aravalli range 
and the plains in between and the Delhi Ridge and its four sections. The Delhi and Noida drains 
fall into the  Yamuna River. The average gradient is of the order of 1 to 4 m/km.  Delhi area is 
generally flat. The Yamuna River is Delhi’s source of drinking water. 
Soil: The soil forming material of the area consists of the alluvium derived from the Aravalli 
through the numerous ephemeral drainage ways and the alluvium derived from the Yamuna that 
consists of the material from the Siwalik and the Himalayas. Dominant influ ence of the Aravalli 
alluvium is apparent in Mehrauli area including a part of the I.A.R.I. (Indian Agriculture Research 
Institute). Yamuna and Aravalli alluvium form the distinct soil forming materials in the area. 
When we consider variation within d ifferent alluviums, texture of the material becomes an 
important differentiating characteristic. Quartz dominates in the sand fraction with iron oxide 
minerals up to 5- 10% and biotite from 5-25%. Quantitative mineralogy of the clay fraction in the 
soil of I.A.R.I. Farm has shown that smectite is the dominant double layer mineral, which is from 
23-40%, followed by mica 10 -28% and kaolinite 12 -19%. Amorphous mineral varies from 6 to 
24%. Presence of smectite and amorphous minerals seem to have their effect o n CEC (Cation 
Exchange Capacity) and available moisture capacity of the soils of the Territory. Thus, mineralogy 
of the soils may be described as mixed. 
Seismicity: Delhi is located in Seismic Zone IV under the Seismic zoning map of India. 
Meteorology and Air Environment : Meteorology: Delhi has an extreme climate, which is very 
cold in winter and hot in summer. The climatic conditions in project area are characterized by a 
rainy season (July -October), winter (November -March) and  Summer (April -June). Long term 
climate data from 199 1-2020 was collected from nearest  Indian Meteorological Department 
(IMD) station i.e. New Delhi (Safdarjang). The maximum daily mean temperature of 44.3° C has 
been recorded in the month of May while minimum daily me an temperature of 3.5° C has been 
recorded in the month of January. The total annual rainfall is 762.3 mm (1991 -2020). The 
maximum monthly total rainfall recorded is 226.8 mm which occurred in August and minimum 
monthly rainfall is 4.1 mm which recorded in  month of November. The maximum mean wind 
speed is 8.8 m/s recorded in the month of June while the minimum mean wind speed is 3.9 m /s 
recorded in the month of November.  
Air Quality: Air quality monitoring was carried out at 12 locations near the corridors. PM10, PM2.5, 
SO2 & NOx concentrations within the study area were found to vary from 100.67 to 154.32 μg/m3, 
54.58 to 72.53 μg/m3, 16.38 to 21.15 μg/m 3, and 22.11 to 30.84 μg/m 3, respectively and CO and

Environment Impact Assessment for Delhi Metro Phase IV-2 Project 
 
 
3 A DELHI METRO RAIL COOPERATION LTD. 
 
O3 were found to be in the range of 0.64 mg/m 3 to 0.86 mg/m 3 and 11.50 to 21.73 μg/m 3, 
respectively. The baseline concentrations for Ambient Air Quality are exceeding the permissible 
limit of NAAQ 2009 standards. 
Noise: Ambient noise levels were monitored at 12  locations. The equivalent noise quality level 
ranged from 60.3 dB (A) to 69.54 dB (A) during daytime and 51.51 dB (A) to 58.93 dB (A) during 
nighttime. The residential zone i.e., N4- Pushp Vihar noise level in the range of 68.22 dB (A) during 
daytime and 57.89 dB (A) during nighttime. The noise levels observed are higher during daytime 
as per CPCB standards. Noise level in N2 - Pushp Bhawan, which has been categorized into 
commercial zone was 65.69 dB (A) duri ng daytime and 56.95 dB (A) during nighttime which is 
exceeding the limits of CPCB standards.  
Vibration: Baseline vibration monitoring was carried out for 24 hours at 12 locations, which are 
adjacent to the proposed metro lines and susceptible to vibrations. The instrumentation used for 
measuring vibration includes NOMIS instrument. PPV was converted into VdB using the formula 
recommended by Transit Noise and Vibration Impact Assessment. Vibration limits specified in 
FTA-VA-90-1003-06 specification s have been suggested for comparison of the results. PPV of 
Ground Vibrations in 3 axes was measured at 12 sampling locations for 24 hours using NO MIS 
Instruments. The values recorded are in the range of 72dB to 80 VdB.  
Water Environment: Water sampling was done at 6 locations for ground water and 6 locations 
for surface water. Ground water quality results show that water will be fit for drinking after 
conventional treatment. i.e., the ground water requires treatment through membrane 
filtration/reverse osmosis (RO) process.  As per report  – “Dynamic Groundwater Resources of 
Delhi” (Central Ground Water Board, New Delhi, March 2023 ), the total annual groundwater 
recharge is 38,152.55 Ham . Out of 34 assessment units (tehsils ), 13 units (38.24 %) have been 
categorized as ‘Over-exploited’, 12 units (35.29 %) as ‘Critical’, 4 units (11.76 %) as ‘Semi-critical’, 
and 5 units (14.71 %) as ‘Safe’ categories of assessment units. 
Hydrology: The project route passes through several drainage channels. The project area is 
located in the floodplain of the Yamuna River, and the frequency of flooding due to the Yamuna 
River overflowing near the project area during the monsoon season is increasing year by year. In 
addition, due to the rapi d urbanization of Delhi and the inadequacy of the drainage system, 
localized flooding often occurs. Zone 0 is a particularly high-risk area within the flood zone of the 
Yamuna River, and part of Route 2 passes through it. Route 1 and 3: The water table depth of the 
Yamuna River floodplain and northern groundwater is 7 -10 m bgl, and in the area of New Delhi 
and the south, where Route 2 passes, it is mainly 14-27 m bgl. 
Ecological Environment: Laying of metro lines and their construction is impacting 15,856 trees 
and flora fauna species as well on Alignment 1 , 2 & 3. Along alignment 1 , 1,971 trees will be 
impacted, while along alignment 2  and alignment 3, 1,500 and  12,385 trees will be impacted  
respectively. During site visit s, common tree species found were Acacia nilotica, commonly 
known as Kikar, Azadirachta indica, recognized as Neem, Ficus religiosa, referred to as Pipal, 
Mangifera indica, or Eucalyptus tereticornis known as Eucalyptus. 
H. IMPACT ASSESSMENT  
The anticipated impacts are categorized into Pre-Construction phase, Construction phase and 
Operation phase impacts. Environment al attributes considered for the impact are Land 
Environment, Air Environment, Soil,  Groundwater Environment,  Surface Water Environment  
Noise Environment, Biological Environment & Socio-Economic Environment. 
Impacts due to Project Location 
 
Project Affected People (PAPs) : The land required for the construction of proposed Metro 
Stations is on Government land and no Private structure will be affected by the project. The

government structures and Land acquired for the project includes Central Government CPWD 
quarters, DDA Land, MCD Parks, Railway quarters, area of Indraprastha Power Generation 
Company Ltd. and Delhi Jal Board. 
Change of Land Use: The project will be developed on government land. The land identified for 
temporary use shall  be returned to  the owning  agencies, after the completion  of the project  
construction. However, change in land use will be done as the existing  dilapidated government 
structure will be demolished to develop the metro line and station.  
Loss of Forests/Trees: Laying of metro line s and construction will impact 15,856 trees. With 
removal of these trees, CO2 absorption is likely to decrease by 0.36 MT and oxygen generation to 
increase by 0.78 MT per year.  
Utility/Drainage Problems: Telephone lines, electric poles and wires, electrical connection 
boxes, gas pipeline, water lines within the proposed project locations may be required to be  
shifted. During the utility shifting , respective service s may be affected due the laying of 
transmission lines. NOC will be required from all concerned departments which own the utilities. 
The Metro lines are crossing 399 light poles, 45 electric poles, 128 main holes, 24 single poles, 1 
telephone pole and 6 HT lines, 6 junction boxes, 3 electric main holes and 1 gas pipeline. During 
the laying of transmission line, activity at a particular area will be impacted, which will however 
be only temporary. 
Selection of disposal site: The project will generate a lot of muck. Improper disposal sites can 
lead to soil and water contamination and hence selection of disposal site is very important. 
Impact due to Project Construction 
The most likely  negative impacts related to the construction  works are mostly  of temporary  
nature. The likely impacts due to construction are; 
• Soil Erosion: Run off from unprotected excavated areas, can result in excessive soil erosion, 
especially when the erodibility of soil  is high. In general, construction  works are stopped 
during monsoon season. 
• Water quality: Ground water contamination can take place if chemical substances get 
leached by precipitation of water and percolate to the ground water table. Dumping of 
construction materials could result in hazardous leachate percolating into ground water, if 
not disposed off properly. 
• Noise Pollution: When a dump truck, excavator,  and pneumatic tool are operating  
simultaneously at a site, the noise levels near the equipment can be significant. Therefore, 
additional protective measures may be necessary for anyone working nearby. 
• Vibration: Vibration level of more than 0.1 inch/second (100 VdB) is found to impact humans 
and structures. Ambient vibrations are in the range of 72 to 80 VdB. 
• Impact due to Land Subsidence: Land subsidence is not anticipated at stations which will 
be constructed by cut and cover method as well as through tunnel boring machine (TBM). 
• Traffic Diversions: During construction period, complete/partial traffic diversions on road 
will be required, as most of the construction activities are on the road. 
• Risk to Existing Buildings:  Construction involves cut and cover, tunnelling and piling. As 
part of pre -construction/construction activities building condition survey will have to be 
conducted.

Environment Impact Assessment for Delhi Metro Phase IV-2 Project 
 
 
5 A DELHI METRO RAIL COOPERATION LTD. 
 
• Pollution due to Transportation of Construction Material and Soil: During the period of 
construction emission due to  truck movement on  account of transportation  of civil 
construction material and disposal/backfill of earth will be generated. Particulate  pollution 
occurs due to excavation,  loading and unloading  of construction  materials, construction 
equipment emission etc. Resulting  pollution is short term. Adequate measures ha ve been 
proposed to mitigate their impact. 
• Increased Water and Energy Demand: The demand for water and energy will increase  
during construction phase. 
• Hydrology:.The installation of bridge piers in the drains and the lack of construction drainage 
channels may affect surface water flow, and flooding may occur during the monsoon season. 
Groundwater: Construction in the underground area may affect groundwater flow. 
Positive Environmental Impacts 
 
Employment Opportunities: In Operation phase, people will be employed for operation and 
maintenance of the system. Thus, the project  will provide substantial direct employment and 
consequent indirect employment. 
Benefits to Economy: These corridors will yield benefits in terms of  
• growth in economic activity due to better accessibility,  
• savings in fuel consumption,  
• corresponding reduction in cost of road construction and maintenance,  
• reduction in vehicle operating costs,  
• savings in travel time, improvement in quality of life and  
• reduction in loss of productivity due to health disorders resulting from pollution and 
accidents. 
Direct Benefits to Passengers:  The project will result in direct benefits to users of Metro and 
other modes: reduction in vehicle operating costs, savings in travel time, improvement in quality 
of life, reduction in loss of productivity due to  health disorders resulting from pollution and 
reduction in road accidents. 
Reduced air and noise pollution:  The metro is expected to off take bulk of road traffic. Thus, 
there are significant reductions of air and noise pollutants due to proposed metro corridors.  
I. ENVIRONMENTAL MANAGEMENT PLAN 
 
The impacts will be mitigated or reduced by incorporating environmental management plan into 
the project. 
Compensatory Afforestation: About 15,856 trees are likely  to be lost, each tree cut will be 
compensated for by planting 10 trees. The plantation sites are not know n as yet. As regards the 
procedure, broadly speaking, after the permission of tree felling is received from Department of 
Forest (DOEF), Government of National Capital Territory of Delhi (GNCTD), land for planting 10 
times the number of trees to be planted will be provided by DOEF of GNCTD since DMRC does not 
own lands. The DOEF of GNCTD will raise a financial demand with DMRC for planting the required 
number of trees and for their upkeep for the next 3 -4 years and DMRC will transfer the amount  
of money prior to initiation of such plantation. 
Use of Energy and Water:  Requirement of electrical energy for climate control, lighting and 
other facilities at stations shall be optimized by proper use of natural day/night light and design

of passenger flow inside stations and on streets outside stations. Rainwater harvesting shall be 
implemented in stations. 
Risk Due to Earthquake:  All structures shall be designed to with stand earthquake of Seismic 
Zone IV. Station design shall be done to facilitate quicker emergency evacuation. 
Housekeeping: Procedures for storage, handling and transport of construction material shall be 
prescribed in SH&E method statement approved for construction. 
Hazardous Waste Management:  It shall  be stored and disposed  of by  the Contractor as per 
Hazardous and Other Wastes (Management, Handling & Trans-boundary movement) Rules 2016. 
Construction and Demolition Waste Management: The construction contractor is required to 
take the measures in accordance with Construction and Demolition Waste Management Rules 
2016. 
Workplace Facilities:  The facilities shall be provided by the Contractor, like: Water supply, 
wastewater and sewage treatment, Solid Waste Management Shelter at Workplace, Canteen 
Facilities, First aid facilities, Day Crèche Facilities, Health care awareness and clinics.  No Labour 
camp is allowed within the construction site.  
Welfare and Safety of Labour:  Construction works shall be executed as laid down  in the 
Conditions of Contract document on Safety Health and Environment (SH&E) to be followed by the 
Contractor and approved by the Implementing Agency. 
Utility Plan: The proposed Metro alignments run along major roads of the city and are required 
to negotiate sub-surface, surface and overhead utility services. Prior to the execution of work at 
site, detailed investigation of all utilities will be undertaken and plans for their retention in situ 
with precautions or temporary/permanent diversions prepared and got approved by respective 
agencies. 
Air Pollution and Noise Pollution Control:  Mitigation measures shall be adopted during  the 
construction period, as given in the DMRC’s contract provision.  
 
Traffic Diversion/Management: Measures such as road widening, traffic segregation, one-way 
movements, traffic diversions, acquisition of service lanes, etc. need to be undertaken. 
Soil Erosion  Control: Excavation shall be limited;  temporary berms and use  of temporary 
mulches, fabrics, mats, seeding, or other control devices or methods may be used. 
Rainwater Harvesting: To conserve and augment the storage of groundwater, it has been 
proposed to construct roof top rainwater harvesting structure of suitable capacity at the elevated 
stations and in the elevated alignment. 
Disaster Management and Emergency Plans: Disaster management and emergency plans will 
be prepared by the Contractor. To ensure proper disaster management, an Emergency Action  
Committee shall be constituted, consisting of Station Controller concerned, Police Officer of the 
area, Home Guard representative, Fire Brigade representative, Health Department representative, 
Department of Information and Publicity, and Non -Governmental Organization of the area. 
Emergency measures will include provision for Emergency Lighting, Fire Protection, Ventilation 
Shafts, Emergency doors. 
J. ENVIRONMENTAL MONITORING PLAN 
During construction stage environmental monitoring will be carried out for air quality, noise 
levels, vibrations, and water quality. During the construction phase, monitoring will be conducted

7 A DELHI METRO RAIL COOPERATION LTD. 
 
as follows: air quality will be monitored 24 hours twice a week at 12 locations till the end of 
construction. Noise levels will also be monitored for 24 hours once a week at 12 locations over 
the same period. Vibration will be assessed 24 hours once a week at 12 locations till end of 
construction. Surface and ground water quality and soil conditions will be checked once every 
four months at 6 locations till end of construction. 
The project authority in coordination with th e DOEF of GNCTD shall monitor  the status of 
ecology/trees along the project corridor at least once a year during construction phase to 
maintain the ecological environment and to monitor the survival rate of planted trees. 
Monitoring of health risk issues that might  arise throughout the project  lifetime will be done. 
Medical Checkups at construction sites will be performed to monitor the potential spread of 
diseases. Regular inspection and medical checkups shall be carried out to workers health and 
safety monitoring.  
During the operation phase, air quality will be monitored for 2x24 hours, twice a month, at 12 
locations for 2 years. Noise and vibration will be monitored for 24 hours, at 12locations, 
respectively, for 2 years . Surface water and groundwater quality will be evaluated once in six 
months at 6 locations for 2 years. 
The project authority in coordination with the DOEF of GNCTD  shall monitor  the status of 
ecology/trees along the project corridor at least once in two yea rs during operation phase in 
order to maintain the ecological environment and to monitor the survival rate of planted trees. 
Monitoring of health risk issues that might arise throughout the project lifetime will be done.  
K. IMPLEMENTATION ARRANGEMENT 
DMRC has the most important role for environment management plan  implementation and up-
dation. DMRC shall carry out periodical monitoring. 
L. GRIEVANCE REDRESSAL MECHANISM  
DMRC has an existing GRM which will be followed. DMRC employs a comprehensive redressal 
mechanism to handle complaints, suggestions, and appreciations. Local communities and 
commuters can lodge their feedback through various channels, including complaint books at 
customer care centres, email, a 24/7 IVRS helpline, social media platforms, and government 
portals or letters. Upon receipt, an acknowledgment is provided in different forms, such as a 
commuter copy for written complaints or an interim rep ly for email complaints. DMRC reviews 
complaints to determine the necessary action. If needed, the complaint is forwarded to the

1.4. Objective and Scope of The Study 
The objective of the study is to carry out EIA study and preparation of EIA report as per 
requirement of the funding agency, JICA.  
In the Ministry of Environment, Forests and Climate Change (MoEF&CC), - previously named 
‘Ministry of Environment and Forests’ -, Government of India, Notification of “14 th September 
2006 and its further amendment”, it is stated that railway projects do not require environmental 
clearance from MoEF&CC.  
As DMRC has planned for funding for the proposed Phase IV-2 of Delhi Metro from JICA, the scope 
of the study is required to be framed according to the requirements of the JICA Guidelines. Thus, 
the Project requires the EIA  & Social Impact Assessment (SIA) to achieve the approval for the 
construction of the project from JICA. This document is the EIA report, while  SIA report was 
prepared in a separate document.  
The scope of the EIA is to: 
• Review previous project/EIA related reports 
• Review the Indian legal framework and international treaty and policy measures to fill 
the gaps with the JICA Guidelines  
• Establish environmental baseline , assess impacts resulting from pre -construction, 
construction and operation phases of the projec t, and safeguard measures for 
protection of environment for sustainable development during project cycles 
• Identify Institutional Plan for Environment Management Plan (EMP) and Environment 
monitoring Plan (EMOP) implementation 
• Conduct meaningful participation of stakeholders and incorporates stakeholder 
opinions into decision-making processes, 
• Disclose information on environmental and social considerations in collaboration with 
project proponent, to ensure accountability and to promote participation of various 
stakeholders.  
• Prepare an EIA report to meet the requirements for environmental and social 
considerations stated in the JICA Guidelines and national laws and obtain approval from 
JICA and Advisory Committee for Environmental and Social Considerations (ACESC). 
1.5. JICA Guideline  
The objectives of the JICA Guidelines are to encourage DMRC as the p roject proponent to have 
appropriate consideration for environmental and social impacts, as well as to ensure that JICA’s 
support for examination of environmental and social considerations are conducted accordingly. 
In its confirmation of environmental and social considerations, JICA places importance on 
dialogue with all involved partners (e.g. the host country, local governments, borrowers and 
project proponents) regarding environmental and social considerations. Wh ile DMRC as the 
project proponent  bear the ultimate responsibility for the environmental and social 
considerations of projects, JICA supports and reviews appropriate environmental and social 
considerations undertaken by the project proponent. This is to av oid or to minimize impacts on 
the environment and local communities caused by development projects, and to prevent the 
occurrence of unacceptable adverse impacts. Transparent and accountable processes, as well as 
active participation of key stakeholders (e.g. local residents and local NGOs affected by the 
project) in all stages of the project are highly considered.  It is important to establish the social 
and institutional framework that allows the reflection and consideration of environmental and 
social costs in decision-making. JICA make clear in their “Guidelines” that the environmental and

1.6. EIA Categorization as per JICA Guideline  
According to JICA Guidelines, the proposed project is classified as Category A. The Project is 
required to be categorized in the sensitive class as a project in the “Roads, railways and bridges” 
sector. This implies it has potential sensitivities similar to a project located in or near sensitive 
areas such as such as areas of National Parks, nationally designated protected areas, or areas with 
cultural, historical or archaeological value. 
Category A: Projects are classified as Category A if these are likely to have significant adverse 
impacts on the environment and society. Projects with complicated or unprecedented impacts 
that are difficult to assess, or projects with a wide range of impacts or irreversible impacts, are 
also classified as Category A. 
1.7. EIA approach and Methodology  
The project has various social and environmental impacts. Such as shifting of high-tension 
electrical wires, tree felling, and generation of sludge. The laying of the metro main will disrupt 
roads, and require tree felling. There may also be inconvenience to various departments and the 
public at locations where pipeline intersects with highways, railways, canals etc. Relocation of 
utilities including gas, sewer, telephone etc will be required which will cause inconvenience to 
the community. Heavy machinery usage at sites could cause noise and air pollution. Furthermore, 
tree cutting  and felling  may impact loca l ecosystems, and poor management and improper 
disposal of construction waste could lead to contamination of local water sources and soil etc. 
Therefore, the project required a comprehensive Environmental and Social Impact Assessment 
and EMP. This involves developing multiple plans for managing potential environmental and 
social impacts for the corridors of the Project. 
The approach is to follow the sequence of steps adopted in an EIA study to ascertain the existing 
baseline conditions and assess the impacts due to pre -construction, construction and operation 
of the project. The approach and methodology adopted for the EIA study includes a desktop study 
of the key project activities and the initial design of the proposed project based on the available 
engineering reports for the project, discussions with the stake holder agencies and review of 
development plans and map s in order to compile relevant baseline biophysical and socio -
economic information about the study area. 
Identification of Encroachments: Identifying instances of encroachment and potential physical 
displacement of communities resulting from the project. 
Accessibility and Barrier Assessment: Analysing the impact of project activities, including the 
construction of metro line networks, on accessibility and potential barrier effects. 
Mitigation Measures: Identifying and proposing appropriate mitigation measures to address the 
impacts of project construction and operation activities.

densely populated subdivision of the city and crosses two railway yards at Sarai Rohilla and New

2.5. Construction Methodology14  
2.5.1. Underground Construction 
For the underground sections running under the road, the cut and cover method of underground 
construction can be employed. However keeping in view the inconvenience to the traffic 
movement, it is proposed to tunnel through by using Tunnel Boring Machine (TBM) or New 
Austrian Tunnelling Method (NATM) in the overburden soil mass. Tunnel excavation for a major 
length of underground section is expected to be carried out by Tunnel Boring Machines. There 
are few stretches along the underground alignment where Cut  & Cover method has been 
considered for construction after Switch Over Ramp (SOR). Tunnel boring machines (TBMs) 
capable of drilling in soft soil with a finished internal diameter of 5.6 m. can be successfully 
employed for boring tunnels through this stratum. The tunnels are proposed with a minimum soil 
cover of 6.0 m15. 
2.5.2. Underground Stations 
All the underground stations have been proposed to be constructed by cut and cover with top - 
down method. The diaphragm walls for such station constructions would be 80 to 100 cm. thick 
and will function as a permanent side wall of the station. It is, ther efore, necessary to construct 
the diaphragm walls ab watertight and with the required concrete strength as has been done in 
other phases of Delhi Metro station construction. By resorting to top -down method the surface

2.5.4. Elevated Structure  
(1) Pre-Cast Construction 
For viaducts segmental pre-cast construction requires a casting yard. The construction depot will 
have facilities for casting beds, curing and stacking area, batching plant with storage facilities for 
aggregates and cement, site testing laboratories, reinf orcement steel yard and fabrication yard 
etc. An area of about 2.5 ha to 3.0 ha is required for each construction depot. For casting of 
segments both long line and short line method can be adopted. 
(2) Launching Scheme 
Launching girder is specially designed for launching of segments. The suggested launching 
scheme is designed in such a way that initially the launching girder is erected on pier head at one 
end of the work. The segments are lifted in sequence and when the lifting is over, they are dry 
matched while hanging from the launching girder.  
Segments are glued with epoxy and pre -stressed from one end. The girder is lowered on the 
temporary / permanent bearings after pre -stressing. The launching girder then moves over the 
launched span to next span and the sequences continue. 
(3) Structural system of viaduct 
The superstructure of a large part of the viaduct comprises of simply supported spans. However 
at major crossing over or along existing bridge, special steel or continuous unit will be provided. 
Normally the Box Girder having a soffit width of about 4.0 m (approximately) accommodates the 
two tracks situated at 4.2 m centre to centre (c/c). The Box Girder superstructure for almost all 
the simply supported standard spans will be constructed by precast pre - stressed segmental 
construction with epoxy bonded joints. 
The standard spans c/c of piers of simply supported spans constructed by precast segmental 
construction technique has been proposed as 28.0 m. The usual segments shall be 3.0 m in length 
except the Diaphragm segments, which shall be 2.0 m each. The other spans (c/c of pier) comprise 
of 31.0 m, 25.0 m, 22.0 m, 19.0 m & 16.0 m, which shall be made by removing/adding usual 
segments of 3.0 m each from the centre of the span. 
(4) Substructure 
The viaduct superstructure will be supported on single cast -in-place RC pier. The shape of the 
pier follows the flow of forces. For the standard spans, the pier gradually widens at the top to 
support the bearing under the box webs. At this preliminary design stage, the size of pier is found 
to be limited to 1.8 m to 2.0 m diameter of circular shape for most of its height so that it occupies 
the minimum space at ground level where the alignment often follows the central verge of 
existing roads.

To prevent the direct collision of vehicle to pier, a Jersey Shaped crash barrier of 1.0  m height 
above existing road level has been provided all around the pier. A gap of 25 mm has also been 
provided in between the crash barrier and outer face of pier. The shape of upper part of pier has 
been so dimensioned that a required clearance of 5.5 m is always available on roadside beyond 
vertical plane drawn on outer face of crash barrier. In such a situation, the minimum height of rail 
above the existing road is 8.4 m. 
The longitudinal centre to centre spacing of elastomeric/pot bearing over a pier would be about 
1.8 m. The space between the elastomeric bearings will be utilized for placing the lifting jack 
required for the replacement of elastomeric bearing. 
(5) Construction of elevated stations 
It is proposed to construct the elevated stations with elevated concourse over the road at most of 
the locations to minimize land acquisition. To keep the rail level low, it is proposed not to take 
viaduct through the stations. Thus, a separate structural configuration is required (although this 
may necessitate the break in the launching operations at each station location) 
Sub-structure for the station portion will also be similar to that of viaduct and will be carried out 
in the same manner. However, there will be single viaduct column in the station area, which will 
be located on the median and supporting the concourse gir ders by a cantilever arm so as to 
eliminate the columns on right of way.

2.6. Maintenance Activities during Operation 
During operation phase, train maintenance activities will be carried out in the main depot cum 
workshops where the overhaul and corrective maintenance facilities for whole fleet are planned. 
The maintenance workshops will be managed by a team of managers w ho will plan, coordinate 
and manage various activities in depot to ensure that the trains are well maintained and cleaned 
for daily passenger service. The main activities that will be taking place in maintenance depot will 
be train washing, filter cleaning, HVAC filter cleaning, bogie cleaning, internal train cleaning, roof 
wash, heavy train cleaning, evaporator cleaning and condenser cleaning.

The proposed metro projects from Inderlok to Indraprastha, Lajpat Nagar to Saket G Block, and

CHAPTER 3. LEGAL, POLICY AND INSTITUTIONAL FRAMEWORK  
A review of the legal and regulatory framework related to the environmental and social in terms of 
their relevance and applicability to the project is presented in this chapter. 
3.1. Applicable Policy, Rules & Regulations to project interventions/activities 
The project's execution will be overseen in accordance with the environmental laws, regulations, and 
standards at both the national and state levels. Additionally, the safeguard policies set forth by the JICA 
Guidelines will be adhered to. These regulations necessitate the avoidance, minimization, and mitigation 
of potential environmental and social impacts. The responsibility for ensuring that subprojects align with 
the legal framework, whether it be at the national, st ate, or municipal level, lies with th e agencies 
responsible for executing and implementing the project. Adherence to these policies is mandatory 
throughout all phases of the project, including design, construction, and operation and maintenance.  
The law on the environment, the "Environment (Protection) Act 1986" has been enacted in India, which 
was established the basic outline of environmental protection. The "National Environment policy" was 
established in May 2006, and the "Environment Impact A ssessment Notification" 2006” on project 
categories for environmental compliance certificate, screening and scoping procedures, public 
consultations, etc. has been enacted in September 2006. These procedures are under the responsibility of 
the Impact Asses sment Division under the MoEF&CC. MoEF&CC, Notification of “14 th September 2006 
and its further amendment”, railway projects do not require environmental clearance from MoEF&CC.  
a. Environment (Protection) Act 1986  
The Environment (Protection) Act is positioned as the Basic Environment Law in India, and explains the 
basic outline of environmental protection, and consists of 4 chapters and 26 items in total. The law 
stipulates the central government's responsibilities  for the prevention, management and reduction of 
environmental pollution. The government is empowered to develop appropriate rules to achieve the goals 
of the Act. The Act defines "Environment" as "includes water, air and land and the inter - relationship 
which exists among and between water, air and land, and human beings, other living creatures, plants, 
micro-organism and property". The Act provides the authority to prevent, regulate and reduce 
environmental pollution and activities which damage environment. The government is empowered to set 
rules in sectors where environmental protection and regulation are required.  
b. Environment Impact Assessment Notification" 2006  
EIA in India is positioned as the primary procedure for reviewing and approving new or modified projects 
under the National environment policy 2006, which was developed under the Environmental (Protection) 
Act. The EIA procedure is stipulated in the Enviro nmental Impact Assessment Notification 2006, which 
includes Requirements of prior Environmental Clearance (hereinafter referred to as "EC"), Assessment 
authority, Categorization of projects and activities, Screening, Scoping and Appraisal Committees, EC 
application, Validity of EC, Post EC Monitoring, and Transferability of EC etc. Various formats have also 
been established in the Notification. There is no EIA ordinance system by regional governments in India. 
The environmental categories of India are divided into three groups, A, B1 and B2 as shown in the table 
below. The criteria between category A and B is relatively clear, but the criteria between category B1 and 
B2 is indefinite. Therefore, it will be judged by screening process. The EC issuance supervisory authority, 
the inspection authority, and other necessary documents are different for each category.  
 
As stated earlier, under the Notification of “14th September 2006 and its further amendment”, it is 
observed that railway and metro projects do not require environmental clearance from MoEF&CC.

3.2. Institutional Frameworks for Enforcement of Environmental Management  
In India Institutional frameworks for enforcement of environmental management relevant to 
Phase IV-2 are summarized below. As per the regulations above, the competent authorities of the 
pollution control will authorize and supervise the project activities of Phase IV-2. Considering the 
cultural heritages, DMRC needs to obtain the project permission and be monitored by the 
competent authorities during construction and operation due to project activities within the 
regulated area.  
3.2.1. Central Government Level 
(1) Ministry of Environment, Forest and Climate Change (MoEFCC)  
The MoEFCC is a central government agency responsible for the formulation, implementation and 
supervision of India's environmental and forestry policy and regulations. It has superior power 
as the highest authority for various permissions and licenses for development activities. 
Considering the relevance of Phase IV-2, MoEFCC may not be the direct authority to authorize 
project activities, but it is the governing ministry of the pollution control boards below. 
(2)  Central Pollution Control Board (PCB)  
Central Pollution Control Board (CPCB) The Central Pollution Control Board is responsible for 
pollution control throughout the country. In addition to the control of air, noise and water 
pollution, it is also responsible for ensuring effective control of disposal of hazardous wastes and 
storage and handling of dangerous chemicals and substances. With the enactment of air and 
water pollution laws, states have set -up their own State Pollution Control Boards (SPCBs) to 
monitor industrial emissions and effluents and to approve the operation of new industries after 
scrutiny. The functions of the SPCBs include:  
• The planning of comprehensive state programs for the prevention and control of air and 
water pollution and to ensure the implementation thereof;  
• Inspection of pollution control equipment/ plans for monitoring of their efficiency  
• The SPCB in consultation with the Central Pollution Control Board may establish norms 
for air quality, gaseous emission and noise level etc.  
(3)  National Monuments Authority, Archaeological Survey of India, and Department of 
Archaeology  
The protection of cultural heritage is very strict in India, and strict management has been 
enforced by the Historic Monuments and Archaeological Sites and Remains (Amendment and 
Validation) Act, 2010.  
 National Monuments Authority is the principal national authority preserving national heritage 
sites and regulating activities of the regulated area. It formulates policies based on the act, 
establishes restricted areas, and approves final permissions for activities in a regulated area. 
Archaeological Survey of India (ASI) is the sole designated authority to investigate the notified 
national heritage sites as per the law. Within 100 m of the prohibited area around any centrally 
protected monument or site, p ermissions for repair and renovation are granted for 
buildings/structures constructed before 1992 or constructed after 1992 with approval from 
Director-General of ASI.  
 Department of Archaeology of the NCT Delhi manages the cultural heritages within the NCT Delhi 
area and the first authority to consult and submit the heritage clearance as per the law. The 
department reviews the application and forwards the clearance appl ications to ASI with its 
review report.

CHAPTER 4. ALTERNATIVE ANALYSIS 
The purpose of analysis of alternatives is to find the most effective way of meeting the need and 
purpose of the project, either through enhancing the environmental benefits of the proposed 
activity and or through reducing or avoiding potentially significa nt negative impacts, so that 
project will become environment as well as people friendly. 
The Delhi Metro Phase IV -2 project has been finalized after considering the environmental and 
social concerns  without effecting the  overall usefulness of the corridor s. Critical categories 
adopted were: 
• Minimum private land acquisition, 
• Least disturbance to properties, 
• Minimum disturbance to people and, 
• Minimum disturbance to ecology/ biodiversity and environment. 
 
The main objective of the study is to ensure that the project addresses the adverse impacts on the 
livelihood of the people during project construction as well as operation stage.  The positive 
impacts of the chosen corridors  are further elaborated in Chapter 7 (Positive impacts). These 
being the over-riding criteria, financial implications of these alternatives were not worked out.

• Traffic Congestion Reduction, Reduction in Number of Buses, 
• Reduced Fuel Consumption, 
• Reduced Air Pollution,

Since, the positive impacts are more than a few negative impacts (i.e. noise and vibration during

The alignment of the corridors are so selected that they will serve the maximum population, will 
entail less private land acquisition, least demolition of private and government structures, least 
tree cutting and will avoid impact on archaeological and his torical structures. To achieve the 
above goals, the alignment suggested is mainly on the central verge of the road. In the highly 
densely populated area the alignment is kept under the ground so as to lessen the social impacts 
that may have resulted from acquisition of property.  
4.2. Alternative analysis 
The alternate analysis has been conducted based on various technical, economic, environmental 
and social considerations for finalization of the routes.  
The Delhi Metro network is almost complete, and Phase IV- 2 is expected to connect the missing 
links. Phase IV - 2 includes not only the extension of existing lines into suburban areas but also 
the construction of sections in the city centre.  
Environmental and social considerations are of utmost importance, and special attention is given 
to depot planning. In the Phase IV- 2, efforts are being made to minimize negative impacts. There 
is a growing trend toward integrating and utilizing existing depots to minimize the need for new 
depot construction. 
In this report, the review is made in several steps. The purpose of the metro corridor is identified 
in the beginning. It is followed by the review of major roads where available road space is 
determined. Routes are proposed based on adequacy of road space. These route options are 
compared with the catchment area of existing metro station. Rout es are adjusted based on 
overlapping catchment area or important historical structures. Final routes are then become the 
metro alignments. These alignments are furthe r analysed, and alternatives are identified by 
project management groups. These alternatives are based on differences in ground conditions 
such as affected buildings, trees, and historical structures. Project details of the alignments are 
determined such as length, alignment curvature, cost, utilities, and others.  
4.2.1. Alignment Planning Factors 
DMRC selected comparison criteria based on the key items that would affect decision making. 
DMRC places higher importance on environmental and social considerations than on profitability 
and technical aspects. Thus the criteria such as ‘Ridership’ or ‘Profitability’ were not selected as 
criteria. The reasons for this are that ‘demand forecasts’ are not expected to show any significant 
differences between alternatives because the alternative proposals are located in the same area, 
and that ‘profitability’ is not a criterion that can determine the validity of the alignment because

(1) Government Plans and Regulations 
a. Expansion of Public Transportation  
Delhi has witnessed significant expansion of its public transportation infrastructure over the past 
few decades, with the DMRC being a key driver of this growth. The DMRC has expanded its 
network to cover various parts of the city. Delhi Metro completed se veral metro lines under 
Phases 1, 2, 3, and construction started for Phase IV -1. Significant portion of the funding came 
from the JICA as a loan to complete these metro lines.  
The Delhi Metro Rail Corporation Act, 2002, is a significant piece of legislation that governs the 
establishment, operation, and maintenance of the DMRC. The Act provides a legal framework for 
the development and management of the Metro System in Delhi. 
The Act empowers the DMRC to acquire land for the metro project through various means, 
however, most of the land required for Delhi  Metro Phase IV-2 are owned by the Government. 
The DMRC is required to follow the procedures outlined in the RFCTLARR Act 16  and JICA 
Guidelines when acquiring lands for the metro project. The SIA outlines the details on this aspect.  
b. Preservation of Natural Environment 
Delhi Metro has made significant contributions to environmental preservation in Delhi. By 
providing a reliable and efficient public transportation system, the metro has helped to reduce 
traffic congestion, air pollution, and noise pollution. The DMRC's com mitment to sustainable 
practices has further enhanced its environmental impact.  
Furthermore, DMRC and JICA have collaborated on several projects. As part of these projects, EIA 
was conducted to assess the potential environmental effects of the metro construction and 
operation. Phase IV-2 is to address the concerns on the environment including the affected areas, 
deemed forests, trees and among others along the project’s alignment.  
c. Preservation of Historical Structures  
The DMRC has taken significant steps to ensure the preservation of archaeological structures 
during the construction and operation of the Delhi Metro. The Delhi Phase IV -2 project, has 
incorporated measures to protect and conserve heritage sites along the metro routes.  
The Archaeological Survey of India (ASI) restricts construction within 100m and regulates those 
within 200m running events. These regulations generally prohibit any activity that could damage 
or disturb archaeological remains. DMRC considered the metro rou tes adjustment to avoid or 
minimize impacts on significant archaeological sites.  
(2) Other Related Policies 
a. Land Use Plans and Phase IV-2 Project 
The Delhi Land Use Plan made by Delhi Development Authority (DDA) is a comprehensive 
document designed to guide the city's urban development. It outlines the desired land use 
patterns, zoning regulations, and infrastructure requirements to ensure sustainab le and 
equitable growth. The key objective of the plan is to promote environmentally friendly practices

“eSampada” is an online platform developed by the Ministry of Housing and Urban Affairs. It

government in managing its vast portfolio of properties. By automating processes, ensuring 
transparency, and improving efficiency, the platform contributes to better governance and 
service delivery.  
Under the Delhi Land Use Plan and Phase IV -2 Project, preparations have already been made to 
manage the government properties including the dilapidated buildings, structurally unsound, and 
those declared inhabitable and abandoned buildings. eSampada delist ed those properties, thus 
several affected government buildings are not occupied before project alignment is finalized and 
constructed.

As a background, Corridor 1 will use the existing depot at Bahadurgarth and Corridor 2 will use

When selecting a location for a railway depot, you can consider factors such as:  
• Accessibility: How close the depot is to the metro alignment localities and how well it 
is connected to existing and future roads  
• Environmental impact: Whether the depot is in an environmentally sensitive area, 
such as a forest or wetland  
• Land availability: Whether there is enough open land for future expansion and 
development including ownership of the land 
• Topographic conditions: Whether the ground is fairly level and how the natural 
ground slopes  
• Engineering geological conditions: How the stability and economic rationality of the 
depot will be affected by the geological conditions

5.2. Land Environment 
5.2.1. Physiography 
The physiography of Delhi is dominated by the river Yamuna, the Aravalli range and the plains in 
between formed by alluvium deposits of recent formation. The Delhi Ridge and its four sections, 
the northern, the central, the south central and the southern c onstitute the farthest extension of 
the Aravalli range, its spurs meeting the Yamuna at two points in the north and the east. The Noida 
or Shahdara area drains from east to west into the Yamuna River. Similarly Delhi and New Delhi 
also drain towards the Yamuna River through various drains such as the Najafgarh drain. The 
average gradient is gentle of the order of 1 to 4 m/km. The Delhi area is generally flat except for 
a gentle rise to form a central ridge from North – East to South – South – West. The Yamuna River 
is Delhi’s source of drinking water. 
5.2.2. Geomorphology 
The Ground water availability in Delhi NCT indirectly relates with its distinct landform units, 
which in turn represent the underlying intrinsic geological features. All the landforms present in 
NCT Delhi can be grouped into three broad geomorphic units: n amely Rocky Surface, Older 
Alluvial Plain and flood Plains of Yamuna River. 
Rocky Surface: The rocky surface represents structurally controlled relict linear ridges and 
isolated hillocks comprising of rocks of Delhi Supergroup. This distinct landform comprising of 
isolated hills is most prominent in the south and south -central par ts and extends from 
Mahipalpur to Wazirabad in the north. Towards south of Mahipalpur the ridge gets bifurcated,

Environment Impact Assessment for Delhi Metro Phase IV-2 Project 
 
 
97 J A DELHI METRO RAIL CORPORATION LTD. 
 
one arm extends towards Mandi and further south while the other arm takes a turn towards 
southeast and extends up to Tughlakabad -Greater Kailash- Nehru Place and Okhla. It attains a 
maximum elevation of 362 Meter above mean sea level which gradually dimini shes towards 
North where rocks are exposed on the Western Bank of Yamuna near Wazirabad. 
Older Alluvial Plain: The gently undulatory terrain on either side of the rocky surface is described 
as Older Alluvial Plain. This surface is separated from the Yamuna Flood Plain by a bluff. 
Depending upon the morphological expressions / features, this un it is further divided into 
different subunits: namely, (i) Najafgarh Older Alluvial Plain, (i) Delhi Older Alluvial Plain and (ii) 
Maidan Garhi Plain. Najafgarh Older Alluvial Plain occupying western and south-western part of 
the region is partly covered by sand dunes and sandy sheets. The gently sloping surface including 
the covered pediment along the eastern flank of the ridge represents the Delhi Older Alluvial Plain. 
Maidan Garhi Plain is a relatively higher plain surface and forms part of Chhatarpur Ba sin. A 
narrow zone of “Badlands” has formed mostly along the western margins of structural ridges due 
to intense development of gullies and rills. 
Flood Plain of river Yamuna: The low -lying flat surface representing the Flood Plain of Yamuna 
River occupying the northern, north -eastern and eastern parts of the NCT is an important 
geomorphic unit. North of Narela, the width of the flood plain varies from 15 to 17 km. The wider 
Older Yamuna flood plain indicates lateral migration of river Yamuna over large areas. This belt 
has good potential for ground water development. It forms the erosional terrace. The Yamuna 
Active Flood Plain represents the wide be lt bounded on both the sides by Eastern and Western 
bunds and is naturally prone to annual / periodic floods being in the floodway and flood fringe 
zone of river Yamuna. It forms depositional terrace and is characterized by abandoned channels, 
cut-off meanders, meander scrolls, point bars and channel bars. The presence of number of cut - 
off meanders -in the Yamuna Flood Plain suggests oscillatory shifting of river. The lakes near 
Bhalsawa, Kondli and Khichdipur are remnants of large meanders.18

5.2.3. Geology 
The rock formations exposed in the National Capital Territory of Delhi are mainly quartzite 
interbedded with thin bands of micaceous schist. These Proterozoic age rocks occur along the 
ridge, extending from Harchandpur (Haryana) in the South to Wazirabad ( Delhi) in the North. 
Quaternary sediments consisting of alluvium deposit directly overlie the Proterozoic rocks. 
Systematic geological and geomorphologic studies carried out by the Geologists of Geological 
Survey of India3 has revealed three Stratigraphic horizons and underlying three distinct 
lithostratigraphic units of NCT Delhi. The highest of these is the erosional surface forming the top 
of denudational hills. The second surface is Older Alluvial plain and the third is depositional 
Younger Alluvial pla in (Yamuna). All three lithostratigraphic units corresponding to them have 
undergone changes due to widespread and uncontrolled urban activity over the period.

5.2.4. Soil Type 
The soil forming material of the area consists of the alluvium derived from the Aravalli through 
the numerous ephemeral drainage ways and the alluvium derived from the Yamuna that consists 
of the material from the Siwalik and the Himalayas. Dominant influe nce of the Aravalli alluvium 
is apparent in Mehrauli area including a part of the I.A.R.I. (Indian Agriculture Research Institute) 
Farm whereas Yamuna alluvium is dominant in the rest of the Territory. Still the influence of the 
mixed alluvium of the Arava llies and the Yamuna alluvium should be expected in some parts of 
the Territory. Wind modification of soils is common. Yamuna and Aravalli alluvium form the 
distinct soil forming materials in the area. When we consider variation within different alluviums, 
texture of the material becomes an important differentiating characteristic. Quartz dominates in 
the sand fraction with iron oxide minerals up to 5 - 10% and biotites from 5 -25%. Quantitative 
mineralogy of the clay fraction in the soil of I.A.R.I. Farm has shown that smectite is the dominant 
double layer mineral, which is from 23 -40%, followed by mica 10 -28% and kaolinite 12 -19%. 
Amorphous mineral varies from 6 to 24%. Presence of smectite and amorphous minerals seem 
to have their effect on CEC (Cation Exchange Capacity) and available moisture capacity of the soils 
of the Territory. Thus, mineralogy of the soils may be described as mixed.19 
5.2.5. Stratigraphic Succession: 
Delhi Supergroup is a part of the Aravalli craton. Delhi supergroup is Mesoproterozoic in age and 
occupied by the rocks of fold belts, alternatively also termed as Delhi fold Belt. The Delhi 
Supergroup constitutes a major portion of the Aravalli Mountain Range and extends over a strike 
distance of about 700 km in Gujarat in southwest to Delhi in northeast, from where the 
supergroup derived its name. The rocks of the supergroup prominently occur in south -western, 
north-eastern and central Rajasthan in the form of a linear belt.

5.3. Hazard and Vulnerability  
5.3.1. Earthquake 
The country has been classified into different zones indicating the intensity of damage or 
frequency of earthquake occurrences. These zoning maps indicate broadly the seismic coefficient 
that could generally be adopted for design of buildings in different parts of the country. Delhi is 
situated in zone IV of seismic zoning map of India. The zone has fairly high seismicity with general 
occurrence of earthquakes of 5 -6 magnitude, a few of magnitude 6 -7 and occasionally of 7 -8 
magnitude. Delhi thus lies among the high -risk areas. Seismicity around Delhi appears to be 
associated with a major geological structure known as the Delhi -Haridwar Ridge. This ridge 
constitutes an important tectonic block between 28O° and 30O° N between 76O° and 79O° E with 
a NE-SW trend. It coincides with the extension of the Aravalli Mountain belt beneath the alluvial 
plains of the Ganga basin to the northeast of Delhi towards the Himalayan Mountain. The first 
recorded major earthquake in this region occurred on 15th July 1720 of intensity 9.0. Subsequent 
other earthquake events occurred in 1803, 1819, 19005, 1934, 1937, 1945, 1949, 1958, 1960, 
1966, 1975, 1980, 1994, of intensity between 7.0 to 9.0.  
5.3.2. Landslide 
The project site is present at no land slide active zone as per land slide incidence map of India. All 
the Project activities will be carried out as per the details provide in the approved project plan. 
5.3.3. Flood 
Delhi is the capital city of India and is situated on the banks of the Yamuna River. Concern for 
floods in Delhi are due the rivers viz. Yamuna Flood Plains. The Yamuna Flood Plains are a vast 
area of land along the banks of the Yamuna River. The Hindon is  a tributary of the Yamuna and 
flows through the states of Uttar Pradesh and Delhi. The Sahibi is a small river that originates in 
the Aravalli Range in Rajasthan and flows through Haryana before entering Delhi, The Najafgarh 
Drain is a seasonal river that  originates in Haryana and flows through the western part of Delhi 
before joining the Yamuna. The average annual rainfall in Delhi is 714 mm with three -fourths of 
it falling in the months of July, August and September. Heavy rainfall in the catchment area of the 
Yamuna can result in a dangerous flood situation for the city. Flooding in the Delhi area can occur 
due to overflow of the Yamuna River, which is prone to flooding during the monsoon season. The 
rapid urbanization and inadequate drainage systems in Delhi also make the city vulnerable to 
localised floods. Delhi has also experienced flash floods in the past, particularly in the low -lying 
areas of the city.

5.5.2. Water resources 
Delhi, being in a semi-arid zone, receives about 61.18 cm annual rainfall and about 81% of this 
rain fall is received during the months of July to September. The balance is received in the 
remaining months of the year. With this low rainfall, Delhi faces significant chal lenges in 
managing its water resources due to its rapidly growing population, urbanization, and limited 
access to natural water bodies. In the past, this limited amount of rainwater was able to fall on 
the forest surface, infiltrate the soil, and be conver ted into groundwater for use by people. Over 
the last few decades, the area of impervious surfaces, like roads, and buildings has increased 
many times in the city, which ultimately prevents rainwater from infiltrating, or soaking, into the 
ground. As a result, a large amount of rainwater over Delhi becomes surface runoff and empties 
into the nearby storm drains. A point of concern is that the intensity of urbanization in Delhi is 
increasing day by day and as a result the generation of runoff rather than groundwater recharge 
will continue to increase in the years to come. 
Delhi relies on various types of water resources to meet its diverse needs. The major types of 
water resources managed and utilized by the Delhi Jal Board and other agencies in the city 
include: (i) Surface water, which includes water from Yamuna River (ii) Water from neighbouring 
states (Ganga River & Bhakhra Storage) and (iii) Ground Water.

The Yamuna River flows along the eastern border of Delhi and serves as one of the primary 
surface water sources for the city. Water is withdrawn from the river and treated at water 
treatment plants before being distributed to consumers. Delhi receives a significant portion of its 
water supply from neighbouring states, such as Haryana and Uttar Pradesh, through various 
inter-state water sharing agreements.  
At present neighbouring states are supplying nearly 86 % of Delhi’s water needs. Consequently, 
the groundwater resource of Delhi is coming under immense pressure, and it is adversely 
affecting Delhi’s water supply condition. However, these sources have also become increasingly 
stressed due to the growing demand from Delhi's expanding population. Moreover, the water 
quality of some of these sources is also a matter of concern due to pollution and inadequate 
treatment. In addition to surface water sources, DJB also manages and extracts groundwater from 
wells and tube wells. Groundwater serves as a valuable supplement to the city's water supply, 
particularly during periods of high demand or scarcity. Rapid urbanization, population growth, 
pollution, and climate change are some of the critical factors that put immense pressure on the 
available water sources. As a result, Delhi has become one of the water deficient cities in the world 
and it is going to become a water scarce city in the future. (Rainwater Harvesting_, Chapter II) 
5.5.3. Hydrogeology and Ground water level 
Various hydrogeological and groundwater exploration studies in NCT of Delhi by CGWB has 
revealed that thickness of fresh groundwater in most of the State varies from 20 to 40 m. It is also 
observed that no fresh water is available in a few pockets in Narel a and Alipur tehsils of North 
District, Saraswati Vihar tehsil of Northwest district, Punjabi Bagh and Patel Nagar tehsils of West 
District, Najafgarh tehsil of Southwest district and Kalkaji tehsil of Southeast District. In one of 
the recent study undertaken under NAQUIM (National Project on Aquifer Management) projects 
by WAPCOS (Water and Power Consultancy Services (India), the granular zones (the aquifers) 
with varied resistivity were picked up from the combined interpretations of electrical resistivity 
(64 inches Normal) and gamma radioactivity logs of the boreholes drilled in the area. In general, 
it is clear that freshwater sediments are followed by the saline water sediments in all over NCT 
of Delhi, the thickness of freshwater sediments is thin in major parts of NCT, Delhi. The depth to 
fresh - saline water interface varies from 10 mbgl to 80 mbgl (metre below ground level). Ground 
water quality below fresh saline water interface is saline all through up to the bedrock. At a few 
locations like Dhansa, Qutabgarh and Bankner, saline ground water is present at a very shallow 
depth range. 
In the Southwest district of NCT Delhi, bedrock is encountered at many places i.e. in Dhansa, 
Samalkha, Kabul lines, Jhuljhuli where fresh/saline water interface also varies greatly across the 
entire area. All along the Najafgarh Drain and two depressions i.e. Gummanhera & Pindwalan 
Kalan, freshwater layer is somewhat deeper i.e. up to 35 mbgl but rest of the area is having thin 
layer of fresh water i.e. up to the depth 25 to 28 mbgl only. In the western parts of the district, the 
thickness of freshwater zone is limited. At a few locations like Dhansa, the saline ground water is 
present at very shallow depths and as we move towards areas in the eastern part of the district, 
where hard rock is present, the thickness of freshwater aquifers is more, and fresh/saline water 
interface occurs at dee per depth i.e. generally around 80 to 90 mbgl. At Rajolkri, the depth of 
fresh/ saline water interface has been observed to be 150 mbgl. 
In the West district, the depth of fresh/saline interface varies from 25 to 50 mbgl. The depth of 
freshwater zone varies from 10 to 45mbgl.  
In South district depth of fresh/ saline water interface varies from 75 to 100 mbgl. The thickness 
of freshwater zone varies from 30 to 85 m bgl. At locations like Gadaipur, Bhatti and Munirka, 
freshwater aquifers are followed by hard rock (Delhi quartzite). In Southeast district at places 
around Madanpur Khadar, the thickness of freshwater zones is limited. Here, freshwater aquifers 
are followed by saline water zone and bedrock encountered at the depth of around 300 mbgl.

(1) Climate  
Delhi is a land locked city. The distance from the sea gives Delhi an extreme type of continental 
climate with the prevalence of continental air during major parts of the year. Only during the 
three monsoon months of July, August and September does the air of oceanic origin penetrate to 
this region and causes increased humidity, cloudiness and rain. The year can be bro adly divided

into four seasons. The cold season starts from December and extends up to end of February. This 
is followed by the hot weather season which lasts till about end of June when monsoon arrives 
over the region. The monsoon continues till the third week of September. The two post monsoon 
months of October and November constitute a transition season from monsoon to winter 
conditions. 
Comfortable weather conditions occur during October to March. During October and November 
weather is very comfortable; and during December and January it is cold with occasional rainy 
days. During February and March nights are cool and the days filled with bright sunshine.22

The maximum daily mean temperature of 44.3°C has been recorded in the month of May while 
minimum daily mean temperature of 3.5°C has been recorded in the month of January.  
The summers in Delhi are very hot and winters very cold. The temperature may rise to about 
45 °C in summers, though the average temperature is around 39-40 °C. There are about 4-6 days 
of heat wave when the maximum temperature of a day rises 4 -6 °C above the normal values. 
Though the winters are not bitterly cold on most of the days, the temperatures may fall to 3-4 °C 
for a few days in winters when the cold winds from the Himalayas prevail over the region making 
the winters chilly. The winters are also marked by mist and fog in the mornings though the Sun is 
often out in the afternoons.

rainfall is received during the monsoon months July, August and September. The rest of the

months. The variation of rainfall from year to year is large.

5.7.1. Protected Area 
Under the Wildlife Protection Act, 1972, it categorised protected areas into four categories: 
National Parks, Wildlife Sanctuaries, Conservation Reserves and Community Reserves.  
A national park is a protected area officially identified by the state government to conserve 
its ecological, faunal, floral, geomorphological, or zoological significance. It is categorised in 
the second schedule of the IUCN list. The power to declare national parks lies with both the

central and state governments, highlighting the joint responsibility for preserving these 
critical areas. 
A wildlife sanctuary is a designated area owned by the government or a private entity, aimed 
at safeguarding specific species of plants or animals, either seasonally or throughout the year. 
A Wildlife Sanctuary has the potential to be elevated to National Park status, but the reverse, 
degrading a National Park into a Wildlife Sanctuary, is not permissible. 
Conservation Reserves can be declared by the State Governments in any area owned by the 
Government, particularly the areas adjacent to National Parks and Sanctuaries and those 
areas which link one Protected Area with another. Such declaration should be made after 
having consultations with the local communities. Conservation Reserves are declared for the 
purpose of protecting landscapes, seascapes, flora and fauna and their habitat. The rights of 
people living inside a Conservation Reserve are not affected. 
Community Reserves are declared by the State Government in any private or community 
land, not comprised within a National Park, Sanctuary or a Conservation Reserve, where an 
individual or a community has volunteered to conserve wildlife and its habitat. Community 
Reserves are declared for the purpose of protecting fauna, flora and traditional or cultural 
conservation values and practices. As in the case of a Conservation Reserve, the rights of 
people living inside a Community Reserve are not affected

5.7.3. Flora and Fauna  
Just 17 of the world’s 190 or so countries contain 70 % of its biodiversity, earning them the title 
“megadiverse.” India is one of these megadiverse countries with 2.4% of the land area, accounting 
for 7-8% of the species of the world, including about 91,000 species of animals and 45,500 species 
of plants, that have been documented in its ten bio -geographic regions. Of these 12.6% of 
mammals, 4.5% of birds, 45.8% of reptiles, 5 5.8% of amphibians and 33% of Indian plants are 
endemic, being found nowhere else in the world. 
(1) Characteristics of Delhi’s Forest Types 
Trees in dry deciduous forests have low height to diameter ratios, produce leaves with low 
specific leaf areas, and have high wood densities. These traits indicate slower and more 
conservative growth strategies in these trees than their evergreen forest counterparts. They have 
adapted to withstand seasonal water stress. The Delhi Ridge represents the Tropical Thorn Forest 
group. The bulk of the native vegetation consists of thorny trees and shrubs that are widely 
spaced and drought resistant. Native species  include Bistendu ( Diospyros montana), Hingot 
(Balanitesrox burghii ), Khair ( Senegalia catechu ), Kumttha ( Senegalia senegal ), Dhak ( Butea 
monosperma), Phulai ( Senegalia modesta ), and Kareel ( Capparis decidua ). The under -storey 
vegetation consists of perennials and annuals that emerge during the rains. The Plantation/TOF 
sub-group includes the trees growing in plantation sites, parks, gardens, avenues, empty lots, 
agricultural lands, etc. Delhi’s forests also fall into the category of “monsoon” forest in accordance 
with the climate. While in rainforests, moisture is available throughout the year supporting 
evergreen vegetation, monsoon forests have a distinct wet and dry season. Trees in monsoon 
forests shed their leaves in the dry season, which begins in late-January or early February in Delhi. 
Most trees flower between March and May; this is when they are leafless, thus making the flowers 
more conspicuous to pollinators. 
(2) Protection of Species by India 
Under the Wildlife (Protection) Act, 1972 , It has six schedules which give varying degrees of 
protection. Schedule I and part II of Schedule II provide absolute protection - offences under these 
are prescribed the highest penalties. Species listed in Schedule III  and Schedule IV  are also 
protected, but the penalties are much lower. Animals under Schedule V (e.g. common crows, fruit 
bats, rats, and mice) are legally considered vermin and may be hunted freely. The specified 
endemic plants in Schedule VI are prohibited from cultivation and planting. The Enforcement 
authorities have the power to compound offences under this Schedule (i.e. they impose fines on 
the offenders).

Delhi's economy is the 13 th largest among India's states and union territories, and is driven by

around 1,650 electric buses managed by the Delhi Transport Corporation (DTC), the highest in 
India and the third highest in the world. DTC has at present existing infrastructure of 35 depots. 
With the introduction of metro services, more travel modes will be available for people. Metro 
and bus services will complement each other to optimise the service to people. Buses improve 
the convenience of public transport as feeder transport to stations, and people can travel using 
buses for short- distance travel and the Delhi Metro for long-distance travel. 
The free travel facility for women in DTC/ Cluster buses has been given by Government of 
National Capital Territory of Delhi (GNCTD) from 29.10.2019. During 2021-22; 13.04 crore (130 
million) free trips in DTC and 12.69 crore ( 126.9 million) free trips in cluster buses were made 
by women passengers. 
Rail: Delhi is a major junction in the Indian railway network and is the headquarters of the 
Northern Railway. The main railway stations are New Delhi, Old Delhi, Hazrat Nizamuddin, Anand 
Vihar, Delhi Sarai Rohilla and Delhi Cantt. The Delhi Metro, a mass rapid transit system built and 
operated by Delhi Metro Rail Corporation (DMRC), serves many p arts of Delhi and the 
neighbouring cities Ghaziabad, Faridabad, Gurgaon and Noida. As of December 2021, the metro 
consists of ten operational lines with a total length of 348.12 km.  
Metro: The Delhi Metro is a rapid transit system serving Delhi, Ghaziabad, Faridabad, Gurgaon, 
and Noida in the National Capital Region of India. It is the world's tenth-largest metro system by 
length of lines. It was India's second modern public transportation system. The network consists 
of 10 colour-coded lines serving 288 stations with a total length of 392.448km. The metro makes 
over 4,300 trips daily. The Delhi Metro's annual ridership was 203.23 crore (2.03 billion) in 2023.

the challenge of managing this influx of traffic and ensuring efficient movement of vehicles. 
As per the Information obtained of accident data from Transport Department, Delhi Traffic Police 
and as per the report of the Ministry of Road Transport and Highways in 2020 crash statistics,  
5,131,714 persons were killed in road crashes in India.  
Road traffic injuries continue to be the leading cause of deaths, hospitalization, and disabilities in 
the country. India has one percent of the vehicle population but accounts for 11 % of all the

(2) Fatal Crashes & Deaths in Delhi

behaviour, economic constraints, poor road markings and signages, defective road design, and

CHAPTER 6. SCOPING 
6.1. Project Phases 
For impacts assessment, the project is divided into three phases pre-construction, construction, 
and post-construction.  
The pre -construction phase focuses on planning and preparatory activities, including project 
design, feasibility studies, land acquisition, obtaining necessary approvals, utilities diversions, 
and awarding contracts. It also involves detailed site surveys and investigations to assess the 
land’s suitability for construction. 
In the construction phase, the physical building of the metro system takes place, including civil 
works such as tunnels, elevated tracks, and stations. This phase also covers the installation of 
electromechanical systems, signalling, and safety mechanisms, along with continuous monitoring 
for quality and safety compliance. This phase also includes involves testing and commissioning of 
the metro systems to ensure they are operationally safe and efficient. 
Once all safety certifications are obtained, the metro is inaugurated and opened for public use, 
with maintenance and operational plans fully established. Operation and maintenance have 
different set of impacts which require management. These phases are interconnected and critical 
to the successful completion of the DMRC project.
